source.title: Large Learning Rates Simultaneously Achieve Robustness to Spurious Correlations and Compressibility
source.authors: Melih Barsbey; Lucas Prieto; Stefanos P. Zafeiriou; Tolga Birdal

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how learning rate relates to held-out performance on standard image-classification datasets, extending the claim's generalization subject. Its main spurious-correlation results concern out-of-distribution performance and are outside the claim.
record.gate_note: The study does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected generalization, adaptive optimizers versus SGD, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Spurious-correlation and compressibility results concern separate outcomes and are not cataloged as rows here. Standard-classification learning-rate results are described in text and shown in figures; precise values are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-rate effects on test accuracy, spurious-correlation robustness, and compressibility. None measures the comparisons or interventions specified in V1–V8. Generalization as a broad topic does not establish a test of these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the standard-classification finding but omits the main conclusion: high learning rates jointly promote spurious-correlation robustness, network compressibility, and favorable representations across varied settings. The authors present evidence suggesting that reduced reliance on hidden or rare spurious correlations contributes to standard-classification gains, and propose confident mispredictions of bias-conflicting samples as a mechanism. They acknowledge that a complete mechanistic explanation remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Varies learning rate and examines standard-classification test performance; does not use the random-label memorization or train-test-gap tests specified in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate; the study reports different generalization behavior across learning-rate settings, but provides no exact values in the supplied text.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher learning rates improve reported standard-classification accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1k within the tested ranges, alongside changes in compressibility and feature utilization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate choice can improve held-out image-classification accuracy and alter learned feature use.

fits_no_version.finding: Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and naturalistic spurious-correlation tasks, higher learning rates jointly improve unbiased or worst-group accuracy, compressibility, and representation properties.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher learning rates can jointly promote robustness to spurious correlations and network compressibility.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: Standard-classification test-accuracy trends are described qualitatively and presented in figures without exact values in the supplied text; the paper does not report train-test gaps for those results.
record.rows_left_out: Spurious-correlation datasets, pruning/compressibility outcomes, representation statistics, and the bias-conflicting-loss mechanism were omitted because they measure OOD robustness or other outcomes rather than the claim's same-distribution generalization versions. Hyperparameter comparisons in Figure 6 were likewise about OOD performance.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out accuracy compared with natural-label generalization under the same architectures and recipes.
Controlled widening beyond the width required for zero training error and the resulting test-error trend.

Convolutional versus fully connected generalization on the specified image tasks, including local connectivity and initialization effects. Cross-architecture spurious-correlation experiments use shifted evaluation distributions and sometimes different training conditions.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning budgets. Demonstrating learning-rate effects separately with several optimizers does not test their relative generalization.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty. Batch-size sweeps concern spurious-correlation robustness and use convergence-based training.
Dropout effects, small-data failures, excessive-dropout underfitting, and removal of dropout together with weight decay under augmentation.

Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of training-test gaps and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. ASAM intervention results and loss-landscape illustrations do not measure this relationship.
Removing examples selected by label-memorization influence, retraining, and comparison with equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The record's T3 classification incorrectly treats a new result about generalization broadly as testing a listed version. Results already declared in rows_left_out do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural labels under the same recipes.
Widening beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test-error comparison and the effects of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD on held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of training-test gaps against other measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
